note: AWRI's typical range is 100-800 mg/L (10-80 g/hL) and the OIV ceiling is 80 g/hL. 10-30 g/hL is only the bottom third of the working range.
The mechanism (skin contact extracting potassium, raising pH) is standard, but no tier-1 source found quantifying orange-wine pH at 3.5-3.8. Recommend 'often above 3.5' rather than a band.

source.quote: [M SO2] = [FSO2] / (1 + 10^(pH-1.8)) ... this adjustment may be calculated to yield free molecular SO2 levels of 0.5 to 0.8 mg/L. In pH range 3.2 to 3.5, this corresponds to additions of 20 to 40 mg/L.

corrected_claim: a molecular SO2 of 0.5-0.8 mg/L needs roughly 25-40 mg/L free at pH 3.5 but 50-80 mg/L at pH 3.8
corrected_sentence: First, skin contact extracts potassium and pushes pH up, so a molecular SO2 of 0.5-0.8 mg/L that needs only 25-40 mg/L free at pH 3.5 needs 50-80 mg/L at pH 3.8 - an uncomfortable figure for a category whose buyers expect low sulphur.
note: 60-80 mg/L free is correct at pH 3.8 (0.99% molecular) but roughly double what is needed at pH 3.5 (1.96% molecular gives 0.5-0.8 mg/L from just 25-40 mg/L free). Attaching one number to a 3.5-3.8 span misstates the low end by about 2x - and the point of the sentence is precisely the pH sensitivity, so it is worth getting right.

note: 70 degrees C was the limit under Article 29d(3) of Reg (EC) 889/2008 and was correct when this question was set in 2021. Since Regulation (EU) 2018/848 took effect on 1 January 2022 the limit is 75 degrees C - stated as such by the European Commission's own 2025 opinion ('heat treatment (up to 75 C)') and by certifier summaries of Annex II Part VI. A candidate sitting today who writes 70 C is quoting a repealed rule.

note: 5-10 g/hL = 50-100 mg/L, and AWRI's published maximum dosage is 100 mg/L (the EU limit is likewise 100 mg/L). AWRI's caveat is worth carrying: CMC only works on wines that are marginally unstable, must follow protein stabilisation, and is unsuitable for reds - all of which the answer already says.

source.quote: As 1 mg/L of oxygen can indirectly result in the loss of up to 4 mg/L free sulfur dioxide, it is important to minimise both the dissolved and headspace oxygen... The dissolved oxygen levels in wine are often reduced to acceptable levels before bottling (generally < 0.5 mg/L) using inert gas sparging techniques.

note: 0.5 mg/L is AWRI's published dissolved-oxygen target, given for pre-bottling rather than for bulk loading; the figure is right, the application is an extension.

These levels are 0.1 g/L for Glucose + Fructose, and 0.05 g/L for malic acid... it is best to aim for a malic acid result of 'not detected', which is usually <0.05 g/L by enzymatic analysis. However, a result of 0.1 g/L or less is low enough for the MLF to be considered complete.

corrected_claim: malic acid at or below 0.1 g/L, ideally 'not detected' (<0.05 g/L)
corrected_sentence: ...malic acid at or below 0.1 g/L - ideally 'not detected', under the 0.05 g/L enzymatic detection limit - where malolactic fermentation is complete;
note: Flagged error class. AWRI's threshold for 'MLF complete' is <=0.1 g/L and preferably below the 0.05 g/L detection limit. 0.2 g/L is four times the detection limit and is not a safe bulk-shipping specification - a shipment sitting warm at sea is exactly where a residual 0.2 g/L would finish fermenting in-tank.

note: Exact match to AWRI's recommended brine/cold test: -4 degrees C for three days (72 hours) on a filtered 150 mL aliquot.

AWRI's 15 degrees C is a bottling/sparging compromise temperature, and WSU reports <15 degrees C limits Brettanomyces growth in combination with molecular SO2 - neither is a published bulk-loading specification. The figure is defensible by analogy but not sourced as written.

No tier-1 source found for a 12-15 degrees C bulk holding specification. WSU reports storage below 15 degrees C limits Brettanomyces when combined with >0.4 mg/L molecular SO2, which supports the upper bound only.

Same TPO problem as th_2017_p3_q1#6 and #22: no tier-1 total-package-oxygen figure found. AWRI publishes dissolved-oxygen pick-up at bottling (0.5 mg/L best practice, 1.0-1.5 mg/L otherwise), which is not the same quantity.

source.quote: The traceability of food, feed, food-producing animals, and any other substance intended to be... incorporated into a food or feed shall be established at all stages of production, processing and distribution... [operators] shall immediately initiate procedures to withdraw the food in question from the market

note: Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 (the General Food Law) is correctly cited: Article 18 imposes traceability at all stages, Article 19 requires immediate withdrawal and notification of the competent authority where food may be unsafe. Both obligations are exactly what a glass-in-bottle complaint triggers.
